National profiles: what is specific to each country?

A consultation tool built on the 55-country experiment (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, one story prompt, 80 stories per country). Everything is relative to the other countries: not how common something is, but how much more or less specific it is to a country than to the rest.

    2. Characteristic values: what is over- or under-represented here

    Each bar is the specificity of a value theme in this country relative to the other 54 (signed z: right, more than elsewhere; left, less than elsewhere). A theme can be common and not specific at all: look at the bar, not at the share. Reasons are the justifications the protagonist gives for what they decide.

    Table with shares and statistics

    Finer-grained reason statements

    The 24 bottom-up clusters of reason wordings (e.g. “Keeping the secret would be betrayal”). Most over- and most under-represented here, with the closest example texts.

    3. Cultural and folklore markers most specific to this country

    Markers are the cultural elements that the judge found in the stories (names, places, food and drink, religious practices, customs, clothing, institutions, language), merged into canonical labels. Evidence = −log10 of the exact probability that a marker with this many stories would land this heavily in this country by chance (higher: more specific). “Generic” markers (spread over many countries, also in the no-country control) rank low.

    Detail

    What “specific” means here

    The question is never “how much of X is there in country C?” but “is X more or less frequent in C than in the other 54 countries taken together?”. A theme such as trust as foundation may be the most common in every country and still not be specific to any of them.

    Categories (decision, ending, protagonist gender, value themes, reason statements). For a country c and a category k the statistic is the share in c minus the share in the other countries. Its p-value comes from shuffling the country labels across stories 2000 times (stories keep their reasons together), two-sided. The z shown is the signed normal equivalent of that p-value (capped at about ±3.5 by the number of shuffles). q is the Benjamini–Hochberg correction over all country × category pairs of the same family.

    Evidence tiers. ◆ beyond chance = q < 0.10 after correction. ◇ suggestive = uncorrected p < 0.05 but not corrected-significant: with this many comparisons several of these are expected by chance. No badge = within noise. These tiers are descriptive and never confirmatory.

    Markers. Each marker counts once per story. The evidence is −log10 of the exact (hypergeometric) probability that, if the stories containing the marker were spread at random over the countries, at least this many fall in this country. q is Benjamini–Hochberg over all marker–country pairs with at least 2 stories.

    Where the data come from

    4,600 stories generated by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (temperature 1.0) from a single prompt that differs only in the country named (80 stories per country, 200 with no country); 4,489 valid stories (stories that switch to Chinese mid-text, are off-task or refuse are excluded). Claude Haiku 5.5 annotated each story in two passes (decision, ending, reasons without knowing the country; cultural elements knowing it). A further pass assigned every reason to the approved list of 17 themes and merged the free-text cultural elements into canonical labels (the original texts are kept in the data).

    Limits

    • One model and one prompt: these are profiles of how this model writes about each country, not of the countries.
    • About 80 stories per country: value profiles are noisy, and most single country × theme differences do not survive correction. Markers, in contrast, are strongly concentrated.
    • The judge is one LLM family; canonical labels and themes are model-assigned. Markers are what the model puts in the story, including stock settings: a marker being “specific” says it is typical of the model’s portrayal, not that it is authentic or accurate.
    • Names and places are counted per story; protagonist, friend and partner names are all included.
